query: Which method can be used for oxidation resistance, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Incorporating oxidation‐resistant alloying elements such as Cr (and optionally Al/Si) into a high-entropy alloy will improve its high-temperature oxidation resistance by promoting the formation of a continuous and protective oxide scale.
generation.material_initial_state: A refractory high-entropy alloy or a Ni-based superalloy without sufficient oxidation-resistant elements.
generation.intervention: Alloying addition of Cr (and potentially Al and Si) to the base alloy composition.
generation.conditions: Exposing the alloy to high-temperature oxidizing environments (e.g., 800–1200 °C) typical of turbine or nuclear reactor conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a dense, adherent oxide scale (e.g., Cr2O3) at the alloy surface.
generation.mechanism: The added oxidation‐resistant elements preferentially oxidize to form stable, protective oxide films that act as a barrier to further oxygen diffusion, thereby reducing oxidation progress.
generation.predicted_outcome: The modified alloy will exhibit a lower oxidation mass gain and improved scale stability compared to the baseline alloy lacking these elements.
generation.baseline: The original alloy composition without sufficient additions of Cr/Al/Si, resulting in poor oxidation resistance.
generation.boundary: This improvement may be limited by excessive alloying that leads to brittle intermetallic formation or at extremely high temperatures where scale spallation may occur.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal amounts and potential synergistic effects between Cr, Al, and Si remain uncertain; exact scale characteristics and longevity under service conditions may vary.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of alloys: one with the standard composition (baseline) and one with additional Cr (and optional Al/Si). Expose both sets to a controlled high-temperature oxidizing atmosphere (e.g., air at 900 °C) for an extended period. Monitor the mass gain and surface oxide morphology over time.
measurements: Surface oxide composition and continuity (using SEM/EDS or XRD analysis)
Adhesion/spallation behavior of the oxide scale
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the alloy with added Cr (or Cr/Al/Si) does not show a statistically significant reduction in oxidation mass gain or fails to produce a more continuous/stable oxide scale compared to the baseline, then the hypothesis is falsified.

Research has proved that RHEAs have excellent mechanical properties at high temperatures, even surpassing the widely used nickel-based alloy [ [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] , [6] ]. RHEAs, with excellent mechanical properties at elevated temperatures, are considered promising high-temperature application materials, which are suitable for complex working conditions such as atomic energy, aerospace, the military industry, advanced nuclear reactors, etc. Previous studies focused on mechanical properties at high- and room-temperatures, but with little research and analysis on high-temperature oxidation resistance [ [7] , [8] , [9] ]. Recently the concept of high-entropy alloys (HEAs), consisting of four or more principle metallic elements in equiatomic or near-equiatomic ratios, has attracted considerable interest owing to its tendency to form solid solution with outstanding mechanical and functional properties [ [1] , [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] , [6] ]. By introducing refractory elements including group IV (Ti, Zr, and Hf), V (V, Nb, and Ta), and VI (Cr, Mo, and W) in HEAs, the developed refractory HEAs (RHEAs) possess high melting temperature, outstanding strength and hardness, high thermal stability, and softening resistance at elevated temperatures, which opens up the possibilities of the alloy developments satisfying structural demands at high temperature.

Since the first WMoTaNb RHEA was reported in 2010, many literatures have been focused on the preparation methods and mechanical properties of RHEAs [ [7] , [8] ]. For example, the BCC WMoTaNb and WMoTaNbV HEAs maintained yield strength of 405 and 477 MPa at 1600 °C respectively, which were much higher than that of Inconel 718 and Haynes 230 [ [9] ].
